title: Student-Selected, Targeted Feedback
author: The Broken Copier
summary: A secondary English teacher describes a feedback routine meant to stay authentic and sustainable with 120 students and the pressure of AI-generated feedback. Students first self-score a short handwritten key moment paragraph against six feedback categories on a sticky note while the teacher explains each lens using exemplars. They then share their writing and scores aloud with a partner of their choosing and highlight one category on which they want the teacher's targeted feedback. The teacher can return that feedback the next lesson, share trends across the class, and invite follow-up conversations at two chairs in the hallway during silent reading. The central argument is that giving students agency at several stages builds their own ability to use the lenses while keeping the teacher's workload humane. The author admits the process is a compromise, a little more efficiency traded for sustainability, and still rejects AI-generated feedback on principle.
points: Students self-score their paragraph on six feedback categories, which trains them to apply the same lenses a teacher would use when workshopping.
A short partner exchange of reading aloud and explaining scores gives students ownership and frees the teacher to check in with anyone who has not finished.
Each student highlights one category for targeted teacher feedback, letting the teacher return useful responses by the next lesson despite 120 students.
Two chairs in the hallway during silent reading created voluntary conferences, with students seeking follow-up feedback in every class period.
The author frames the routine as a trade-off that favors sustainability and rejects AI-generated feedback while holding generosity toward oneself.
quotes: The ultimate goal here,” I say, “is for you to internalize these lenses—for you to be able look for these different things in your own piece without me sitting alongside you.

When students return to their seat, they highlight one category on their sticky note that they would like me to provide targeted feedback on. By doing this, students give me a clear direction to focus my feedback towards once I collect their written pieces with sticky notes attached.

However, with 120 students and quite-limited time, this sequence does three important things: (a) it shifts the ownership in the process to students as far as how they see and understand their own work; (b) it helps me design my own instruction with better alignment towards what I’m asking of students; and (c) it allows students agency in multiple stages—including what feedback they want from me.
But I’m able to turn around this targeted feedback the very next lesson in a way that I would not be able to if I tackled each category of feedback comprehensively.

In classes of 30+ students, conferencing with every single one of students in a given lesson is incredibly difficult. So is offering thoughtful, comprehensive feedback to 120 pieces of student writing—even short constructed responses like this one.
Authentic, quality feedback matters but authentic, quality feedback takes time, too. That time takes a toll.
we need to hold generosity towards ourselves in one hand while clinging tight to our values in the other.
context: The teacher states the purpose of the self-scoring step, which is to move the feedback lenses from the teacher's head into the students' own habits.
This passage describes the core mechanism, in which a student's choice of one category directs and narrows the teacher's response.
The author justifies the routine by naming three benefits, covering student ownership, better instructional alignment, and agency at several stages.
He argues that narrowing the feedback focus is what makes quick turnaround feasible at his class sizes, despite the process being imperfect.
The passage establishes the workload problem that motivates the routine and explains why teachers are tempted by automated feedback tools.
The author names the tension between feedback quality and teacher sustainability that underlies his compromise approach.
His closing takeaway frames the routine as a balance between self-compassion about limits and firm commitment to authentic feedback.
